title: Activating mutations in EGFR and PI3K promote ATF4 induction for NSCLC cell survival during amino acid deprivation
author: Mizuki Takahashi; Yuka Okamoto; Yu Kato; Hitomi Shirahama; Satomi Tsukahara; Yoshikazu Sugimoto; Akihiro Tomida
text:
Abstract
Some oncoproteins along with stress kinase general control non-derepressible 2 (GCN2) can ensure the induction of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) to counteract amino acid deprivation; however, little is known regarding the role of the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K pathway. In this study, we demonstrate that both mutated EGFR and PIK3CA contribute to ATF4 induction following GCN2 activation in NSCLC cells. The inhibition of EGFR or PI3K mutant proteins, pharmacologically or through genetic knockdown, inhibited ATF4 induction without affecting GCN2 activation. A downstream analysis revealed that the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K pathway may utilize mTOR-mediated translation control mechanisms for ATF4 induction. Furthermore, in NSCLC cells harboring co-mutations in EGFR and PIK3CA, the combined inhibition of these oncoproteins markedly suppressed ATF4 induction and the subsequent gene expression program as well as cell viability during amino acid deprivation. Our findings establish a role for the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K pathway in the adaptive stress response and provide a strategy to improve EGFR-targeted NSCLC therapy.
Keywords: NSCLC, ISR, ATF4, Oncogenic mutation, EGFR, PI3K

1. Introduction
The integrated stress response (ISR) is an adaptive mechanism that cells utilize to manage intrinsic and extrinsic stress conditions. In response to various types of stress, the ISR pathway is activated by the activity of four eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α) kinases, including general control non-derepressible 2 (GCN2), protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), heme-regulated inhibitor (HRI), and protein kinase R (PKR) [1,2]. Of these kinases, GCN2 is specifically activated in response to amino acid deprivation and its activation occurs through binding of uncharged tRNAs, resulting from a reduction in amino acid attachment by aminoacyl tRNA synthetases [3]. Inhibitors of aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, such as L-Histidinol (His; histidyl-tRNA synthetase inhibitor) and halofuginone (HF; prolyl-tRNA synthetase inhibitor), activate GCN2 by mimicking an amino acid-deprived state [4,5]. Once activated, GCN2 and other eIF2α kinases phosphorylate eIF2α on serine 51, resulting in reduced global translation and increasing translation of activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) using upstream open reading frames (uORFs) [6,7]. ATF4 subsequently promotes the transcription of stress response genes, such as amino acid metabolic processes as a survival response [8]. In the event of severe and prolonged stress, the stress-signaling pathway can initiate a pro-apoptotic response [9].
The ISR plays an important role in ameliorating various types of tumor-associated cellular stress, such as nutrient deficiency and proteotoxic stress, and may be involved in tumorigenesis, tumor progression, and resistance to therapy [10]. For example, elevated GCN2 expression has been observed in various tumor types [11] and tumor growth in xenograft models may be inhibited by knockdown of GCN2 and ATF4 [12]. The GCN2-ATF4 branch of the ISR also plays an important role in angiogenesis [13], reprogramming of amino acid metabolism [12,14,15], and reactive oxygen species homeostasis during tumor growth [16]. Consistent with the contribution of ISR to tumorigenesis, several driver oncogenes, such as KRAS, BRAF, and BCR-ABL, interact with the ISR signaling pathway, which results in the upregulation of ATF4. For example, inhibition of BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia cells prevents activation of the GCN2-ATF4 and PERK-ATF4 branches of the ISR, rendering the cells sensitive to amino acid deprivation and ER stress conditions, respectively [17]. Likewise, inhibition of activated BRAF in melanoma cells and activated KRAS in NSCLC cells prevent ATF4 induction during amino acid deprivation [18,19]. Therefore, in cancer cells harboring activating mutations, the oncogenic signal often contributes to regulation of the ISR, and the inhibition of oncogenic signal can provide a strategy to modulate the ISR under nutrient deprivation.
In NSCLC, activating EGFR mutations are observed in approximately 30%–50% of Asian and 10%–15% of Caucasian patients [20,21]. EGFR regulates cell growth and survival and promotes tumor development by activating downstream signal cascades, such as the RAS-RAF-MEK-MAP and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways [22]. Interestingly, activating mutations in PIK3CA, which encodes the p110α catalytic subunit of PI3Ks, occur in approximately 2%–5% of NSCLC patients [23] and co-alteration of PIK3CA has been documented in 9%–12% of EGFR-mutated lung tumors [24]. Although somewhat controversial, the co-existence of EGFR and PIK3CA mutations is associated with resistance to EGFR-targeted therapy in NSCLC patients [[25], [26], [27]]. Several studies have suggested that EGFR signaling as well as its signal transducers are associated with the ISR. Moreover, ligand-mediated activation of the EGFR pathway and activity of the PI3K pathway may ensure the activation of the PERK branch of the ISR [28,29]. We have also demonstrated that the mTOR pathway mediates the regulation of the ISR, downstream of oncogenic signals, such as BRAF and BCR-ABL [17,18]; however, it remains unclear how oncogenic mutations in EGFR and PIK3CA regulate the ISR pathway.
In this study, we demonstrate that the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K pathway regulates ATF4 induction and cell survival during amino acid deprivation in NSCLC cells. Pharmacologic inhibition and genetic knockdown revealed that mutated EGFR and PIK3CA contribute to ATF4 induction during activation of the GCN2 branch of the ISR. Depending on the mutational status, NSCLC cells experiencing amino acid deprivation conditions exhibit sensitization to the inhibition of EGFR or combined inhibition of EGFR and PI3K. Our findings also suggest that co-mutations in EGFR and PIK3CA may be advantageous for maintaining metabolic homeostasis in NSCLC cells by regulating ATF4 induction.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Cell lines and reagents
The human non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines NCI–H1975 (H1975), HCC827, NCI–H460 (H460), and A549 were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA). Cell authentication was confirmed by short tandem repeat analysis at the ATCC. PC9 was a kind gift from Dr. Kakiuchi, Tokushima University. The mutational status of EGFR and PIK3CA in these cell lines is shown in Table 1. The cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 (Wako, Osaka, Japan) supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS; Corning, NY, USA) and 100 μg/mL kanamycin (Meiji Seika Pharma Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. All cell lines were used for no more than 20 passages after thawing. Osimertinib, alpelisib, buparlisib, copanlisib, GSK2636771, MK2206, trametinib, rapamycin, PP242, halofuginone (HF) (Selleckchem, Houston, TX, USA), GCN2iB (MedChemExpress, Monmouth, NJ, USA), and silvestrol (ChemScene, Monmouth, NJ, USA) were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (Wako) as a stock solution. l-Asparaginase (ASNase; Kyowa Kirin Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan), L-Histidinol dihydrochloride (His), and puromycin (Sigma-Aldrich, Tokyo, Japan) were dissolved in sterilized distilled water. For glutamine deprivation experiments, cells were cultured with RPMI-1640 without glutamine (183–02165, Wako) supplemented with 10% FBS and kanamycin. All the materials used in this study are shown in Key resources table in Supplementary Material.

2.2. Immunofluorescence staining and detection of apoptotic cells
Immunofluorescence staining for ATF4 was performed as described previously [30]. Cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde-phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (Wako) for 15 min and permeabilized with PBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100 and 5% bovine serum albumin for 1 h. After incubation with primary [anti-ATF4 antibody (#11815, Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA)] and secondary [Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated goat anti-rabbit antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MS, USA)] antibodies, the nuclei were counterstained with Hoechst 33342 solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific). For the detection of apoptotic cells, nuclei staining of live cells was done with Hoechst 33342 diluted in Live Cell Imaging solution (Thermo Fischer Scientific). Images were acquired and analyzed using the IN Cell Analyzer 6000 and IN Cell Developer Toolbox software (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA, USA) or by Operetta CLS™ and Harmony High-Content Imaging and Analysis Software (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MS, USA). Induction of ATF4 was determined by setting nuclear ATF4 intensity under normal conditions at 100%. Compound-dependent inhibition of ATF4 induction was determined by calculating the increase in nuclear ATF4 signal intensity during amino acid deprivation compared with normal conditions and setting it at 100%. Apoptosis induction was calculated by dividing the number of nuclear fragmentations by the total number of nuclei.
2.3. Immunoblot analysis
Immunoblot analysis was performed as described previously [31]. The cells were lysed with sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) lysis buffer (62.5 mM Tris-HCl, pH 6.8, 2% SDS, 50 mM dithiothreitol, 10% glycerol) and protein concentrations were determined using the Bio-Rad protein assay (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). Protein samples were resolved on a polyacrylamide gel with a 4%–20% gradient (Cosmo Bio Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes (Cytiva). The membranes were probed with first and secondary antibodies, and the specific signals were detected using Western Lightning Plus-ECL (PerkinElmer). The following antibodies were used: ATF4 (#11815), PI3K p110α (#4249), PI3K p110β (#3011), PI3K p110δ (#34050), p-EGFR (Tyr1068, #3777), EGFR (#4267), p-AKT (Ser 473, #4060), AKT (pan, #4685), p-eIF2α (Ser 51, #3398), p-4EBP1 (Ser 65, #9456), 4EBP1 (#9644), RPS3 (#9538), p-MEK1/2 (Ser 217/221 #9121), MEK1/2 (#8727), RAPTOR (#2280), and RICTOR (#9476) were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology. p-GCN2 (Thr 899, ab75836), GCN2 (ab134053), EIF2S1 (eIF2α, ab5369), and PSAT (ab154055) were purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, MA, USA). Anti-β-actin antibody (A5441) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Horseradish peroxidase (HRP)–linked donkey anti-rabbit immunoglobulin G (IgG) secondary antibody (NA934V) and HRP–linked sheep anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (NA931V) were purchased from Cytiva.
2.4. Cell proliferation assay
Cells were seeded into a 96-well plate. The following day, the cells were treated with the indicated concentrations of compounds for 72 h. Cell viability was determined based on intracellular ATP content using the Cell Titer-Glo 2.0 Cell Viability Assay (Promega, Madison, WI, USA). Relative cell viability under each condition was defined as the percentage of the appropriate control condition.
2.5. RNA interference
Dharmacon ON-TARGETplus SMART pool siRNAs against non-targeting control (D-001810-10), PIK3CA (L-003018-00), PIK3CB (L-003019-00), PIK3CD (L-006775-00), RPTOR (L-004107-00), and RICTOR (L-016984-00) were purchased from Horizon Discovery (Lafayette, CO, USA). Each siRNA was transfected into 2 × 105 cells in a 6-well plate at a final concentration of 20 nM by reverse transfection with Lipofectamine® RNAiMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific).
2.6. Quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis
Total RNA was isolated from cells using the RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Quantitative RT-PCR was performed using the StepOne™ real-time detection system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with the SuperScript Ⅲ Platinum SYBR Green One-Step qRT-PCR kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Primer sequences were as follows: ATF4-forward: 5′-CCTGTCCTCCACTCCAGATC-3′, ATF4-reverse: 5′-CACTGAGGGATCATGGCAAC-3′, Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH)-forward: 5′-AAGGTGAAGGTCGGAGTCAA-3′, and GAPDH-reverse: 5′-AATGAAGGGGTCATTGATGG-3’. The mRNA expression levels of ATF4 were normalized to GAPDH expression and relative expression levels of ATF4 mRNA were calculated by setting the levels under normal conditions as 1.
2.7. Assessment of protein synthesis
The global translational activity of cells was assessed using a non-radioactive method as described previously [32]. After compound treatment, the cells were cultured for 30 min in the presence of 1 μg/mL puromycin. Puromycin incorporation was determined by immunoblotting with an anti-puromycin antibody (#EQ0001, Kerafast, Boston, MA, USA).
2.8. Transcriptome analysis
Microarray analysis was performed using the Affymetrix GeneChip Human Genome U133 Plus 2.0 array (Thermo Fisher Scientific) as described previously [33]. The data were normalized by the Robust Multichip Average method using the affy package of the R-based Bioconductor software. After replacement of the signal intensity less than 50 to 50, differentially expressed genes (DEGs), in which expression was up- or down-regulated more than 2-fold compared with control conditions, were selected. Hierarchical clustering was performed using Gene Cluster 3.0 and visualized by Java TreeView. Pathway analysis and TRRUST analysis were carried out by Enrichr (maayanlab.cloud) [[34], [35], [36], [37]]. The transcriptome data used in this study were submitted to the National Center for Biotechnology Information Gene Expression Omnibus (GSE216508).
2.9. Data reproducibility
All data except for transcriptome analysis were confirmed to be reproducible by repeating more than twice.
2.10. Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed with GraphPad Prism 9 software (GraphPad Software, Boston, MA, USA), except for transcriptome analysis (described above). Fig. S3The one-way (Fig. 6) or two-way (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 7, and Fig. S3) analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed for comparisons between gourps, followed by Dunnett's test as post-hoc analysis. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
3. Results
3.1. Osimertinib suppresses ATF4 induction in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells
Using the third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) osimertinib, we determined the effects of EGFR inhibition on the induction of ATF4 during amino acid deprivation in NSCLC cell lines harboring EGFR activating mutations (Table 1). In the EGFR-mutated HCC827, PC9 and H1975 cells, osimertinib similarly suppressed EGFR phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner at 10 nM or above (Fig. S1a). The conditions of amino acid deprivation were established by adding L-Histidinol (His; inhibitor of histidyl-tRNA synthetase) or l-Asparaginase (ASNase; depleting extracellular asparagine) at 1 U/ml into the culture medium. For His, the equitoxic concentrations were predetermined to be 1 mM for particularly sensitive cells (HCC827 and PC9) and 2 mM for others. Under these conditions, treatment with 10 nM osimertinib suppressed ATF4 induction in HCC827 and H1975 cells as evidenced by immunofluorescence staining and immunoblot analyses (Fig. 1a and b). Similarly, osimertinib suppressed ATF4 induction in PC9 cells under ASNase-induced stress conditions (Fig. S1b) and in HCC827 and H1975 cells under glutamine-deprived conditions (Fig. S2a). The effects of osimertinib tended to be more pronounced in HCC827 cells compared with H1975 cells, especially under ASNase-induced stress conditions. Actually, in H1975 cells, osimertinib had little effect at 10 nM (data not shown), and higher concentrations (200 and 500 nM) were required to inhibit ASNase-induced ATF4 expression (Fig. 1b). Of note, osimertinib barely affected ASNase-induced activation (phosphorylation) of GCN2 and subsequent phosphorylation of eIF2α in both cell lines (Fig. 1b). In contrast, GCN2iB, a GCN2-specific inhibitor [15], suppressed GCN2 activation as well as ATF4 induction (Fig. 1c). These inhibitory effects of osimertinib on ATF4 induction were not observed in H460 and A549 cells expressing wild-type (WT) EGFR, even at 1 μM, which is the clinically achievable maximum steady-state concentration, although ATF4 inducibility under each stress condition was comparable regardless of EGFR mutation status (Fig. 1d, Fig. S1c, and S1d). Thus, osimertinib selectively inhibits ATF4 induction in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cells without affecting GCN2 activation.
Next, we examined cell sensitivity to osimertinib under normal and stress conditions by assessing ATP-based cell viability and apoptosis induction (Fig. 1e–g). Treatment with osimertinib for 72 h reduced the viability of EGFR-mutant (mut) PC9, HCC827, and H1975 cells in a dose-dependent manner over a similar range of concentrations, but not in EGFR-WT H460 cells even at higher concentrations (Fig. 1e). This is consistent with the observation that osimertinib selectively inhibits EGFR with TKI-sensitizing and T790M-resistant mutations [38]. Osimertinib sensitivity was enhanced under His-induced stress conditions compared with normal conditions in all three EGFR-mut cell lines, but to a lesser extent in H1975 compared with HCC827 and PC9 cells. Similarly, the induction of apoptosis after a 48-h treatment with osimertinib was more pronounced in HCC827 compared with H1975 cells under His- and ASNase-stress conditions (Fig. 1f and g). Collectively, these results suggest that inhibition of the ISR is associated with increased cell death by osimertinib treatment during amino acid deprivation.
3.2. PI3K inhibition suppresses ATF4 induction effectively in PIK3CA-mutant cells
H1975 cells, which are tolerant to ATF4 induction inhibition by osimeritinib as described above, harbor the PIK3CA activating mutation G118D [39] in addition to EGFR mutations (Table 1). PIK3CA encodes p110α, one of three catalytic p110 subunits (α, β, and δ) of Class-1A PI3Ks, which heterodimerize with a regulatory p85 subunit to exert PI3K activity [40]. Interestingly, alpelisib, a PI3K p110α-specific inhibitor, suppresses ATF4 induction in PIK3CA-mut H1975, but was less effective in PIK3CA-WT HCC827 cells under ASNase- and His-induced stress conditions as well as under glutamine deprivation conditions (Fig. 2a and Fig. S2b). Similarly, a pan-PI3K inhibitor copanlisib suppressed ATF4 induction more effectively in H1975 cells compared with HCC827 cells (Fig. 2b). However, the inhibitory effects of another pan-PI3K inhibitor, buparlisib, on ATF4 induction were comparable in both cells, which may be related to its inhibitory effect on mTOR activity [41] (see below), as evidenced by the strong dephosphorylation of 4EBP1 (Fig. 2b). As previously observed [42,43], phosphorylation levels of 4EBP1 were moderately declined under ASNase-induced stress conditions, whereas the PI3K inhibitors effectively reduced 4EBP1 phosphorylation under both normal and stress conditions (Fig. 2b). Collectively, these results indicate that in contrast to osimertinib, PI3K inhibitors exhibit a greater inhibitory effect on ATF4 induction in PIK3CA-mut H1975 compared with PIK3CA-WT HCC827 cells.
We also found that PIK3CA-mut inhibition prevented ATF4 induction even in the EGFR-WT cellular context. Alpelisib suppressed ATF4 induction in PIK3CA-mut H460, but not in PIK3CA-WT A549 cells under His-induced stress conditions (Fig. 2c). In contrast, the p110β-specific inhibitor GSK2636771 did not suppress ATF4 induction in H1975 cells under ASNase- and His-induced stress conditions (Fig. 2d). With respect to downstream signaling, ATF4 induction in H1975 cells under ASNase-induced stress conditions was prevented by the allosteric AKT inhibitor MK2206 (more effectively compared with HCC827 cells), but not by the MEK inhibitor trametinib (Fig. 2e and f), indicating the importance of the PI3K-AKT axis in ATF4 regulation.
To further confirm the isoform-specific involvement of the PI3K catalytic p110 subunit in ATF4 regulation, we knocked down PIK3CA (p110α), PIK3CB (p110β), and PIK3CD (p110δ) in H1975 and HCC827 cells using specific siRNAs targeted to each subunit. Similar to alpelisib treatment, PIK3CA knockdown suppressed ATF4 induction under His- and ASNase-induced stress conditions more effectively in H1975 cells compared with HCC827 cells without affecting GCN2 activation (Fig. 3a). In contrast, neither PIK3CB nor PIK3CD knockdown suppressed ATF4 induction in H1975 cells (Fig. 3b). These results demonstrate that in PIK3CA-mut cells, the p110α-mediated PI3K pathway regulates ATF4 induction, possibly through different mechanisms from the GCN2-mediated branch of the ISR.
3.3. Involvement of mTOR in ATF4 regulation downstream of PI3K
mTOR is an important downstream mediator of PI3K-AKT signaling and functions by forming the multiprotein complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2 [44]. To determine the role of mTOR in ATF4 regulation during amino acid deprivation, we knocked down RAPTOR and RICTOR, specific and essential components of mTORC1 and mTORC2, respectively. Similar to PIK3CA knockdown above, knockdown of RAPTOR and RICTOR suppressed ATF4 induction more effectively in H1975 compared with HCC827 cells under ASNase-induced stress conditions (Fig. 4a and b). Although somewhat variable, similar inhibitory effects on ATF4 induction under ASNase- and His-induced stress conditions were observed with rapamycin, an allosteric inhibitor of mTORC1 (Fig. 4c and e) and PP242, an mTOR kinase inhibitor that can suppress both mTORC1 and mTORC2 activity (Fig. 4d and f).
We further addressed the mechanisms of ATF4 regulation by the PI3K-mTOR pathway in H1975 and HCC827 cells. As previously reported [45,46], our quantitative RT-PCR showed that ATF4 mRNA levels were increased 2- to 2.5-fold under His- or ASNase-induced stress conditions compared to normal conditions in both H1975 and HCC827 cells. PIK3CA knockdown only had a slight effect on ATF4 mRNA expression under His- and ASNase-induced stress conditions as well as normal conditions (Fig. 5a). In contrast, global translation activity, as determined by puromycin incorporation, was reduced by PIK3CA knockdown more substantially in H1975 cells compared with HCC827 cells under normal and ASNase-induced stress conditions (Fig. 5b). Translation control by the mTOR signaling pathway occurs primarily through control of the eIF4F (eukaryotic initiation factor 4 F) initiation complex [44,47]. Consistent with this fact, silvestrol, an inhibitor of the RNA helicase eIF4A in eIF4F complex [48], suppressed ATF4 induction in a dose-dependent manner under His-induced stress conditions at lower concentrations in H1975 cells compared with HCC827 cells (Fig. 5c). These results suggest that the control of eIF4F-mediated translation initiation by mTOR signaling is involved in ATF4 regulation downstream of PIK3CA.
3.4. Combined effects of EGFR and PI3K on ATF4 induction and cell survival
Because oncogenic mutations in both EGFR and PIK3CA contribute to the upregulation of ATF4, we examined the combined effects of EGFR and PI3K inhibition. In these experiments, we used alpelisib at the relatively low concentration of 1 μM to avoid excessive cytotoxicity of the agent alone. Compared with either the EGFR inhibitor osimertinib or the PI3K inhibitor alpelisib alone, the combination exhibited enhanced inhibitory effects on ATF4 induction in H1975 cells under His-induced stress conditions, whereas no such enhancement occurred in HCC827 cells (Fig. 6a). Similar results were obtained under stress conditions with halofuginone (HF) and glutamine deprivation (Fig. 6b and Fig. S2c) and in the combination of osimertinib and another PI3K inhibitor copanlisib in His-induced stressed H1975 cells (Fig. 6c). In contrast, ATF4 mRNA levels were barely altered by osimertinib, alpelisib, or their combination in H1975 and HCC827 cells both under normal and stress conditions (Figs. S3a–c).
Transcriptome analysis of H1975 cells treated with osimertinib, alpelisib, or both under normal and His-induced stress conditions revealed that the combination of both inhibitors, with or without stress, significantly altered the expression of a variety of genes, as shown by hierarchical clustering (2816 probes for 2133 genes) (Fig. 6d). In contrast, treatment with the chemical stressor His yielded relatively few DEGs (156 probes for 125 genes) (Fig. 6e). Among the His-associated DEGs, we identified a cluster designated the Stress-EGFR/PI3Ki signature (22 probes for 21 genes). It consisted of His-stress-inducible genes, in which induction was markedly inhibited by the combination of osimertinib and alpelisib, but only partially by each inhibitor alone (Fig. 6e). A bioinformatics analysis revealed that the Stress-EGFR/PI3Ki signature was significantly associated with amino acid metabolism, mTORC1 signaling, and the unfolded protein response pathways (Table 2, Table 3) and may be regulated by ATF4 according to the TRRUST database [37] (Table 4). Indeed, we confirmed that the induction of phosphoserine aminotransferase (PSAT), a known target of ATF4 [49] in the Stress-EGFR/PI3Ki signature, was markedly inhibited by the combination of osimertinib and alpelisib in H1975 cells exposed to His-induced stress (Fig. 6f). Interestingly, the combination markedly inhibited EGFR phosphorylation compared with each inhibitor alone (Fig. 6f), suggesting that EGFR and PI3K may strongly modulate ATF4 induction through the maintenance of oncogenic signals interdependently.

We found that the combination of osimertinib and alpelisib, compared with each alone, exhibited enhanced cytotoxicity in H1975 cells even under normal conditions, but more effectively under stress conditions of His and HF (Fig. 7a and b). Similarly, the combination of osimertinib and alpelisib induced apoptosis in H1975 cells more potently under His-induced stress compared with normal conditions (Fig. 7c). Taken together, these results indicate that oncogenic EGFR and PI3K cooperate and contribute to cell survival under conditions of amino acid deprivation, possibly by upregulating ATF4 expression.
4. Discussion
In this study, we demonstrated that oncogenic mutations in both EGFR and PIK3CA contribute to the cellular adaptive response under conditions of amino acid deprivation. Specifically, both oncogenic proteins activate the ISR pathway, which can lead to metabolic reprogramming to adapt to amino acid imbalances. EGFR inhibition selectively prevented induction of the ISR transcription factor ATF4 in NSCLC cells harboring EGFR mutations. Similarly, ATF4 induction was suppressed by PI3K inhibition in PIK3CA mutant cells compared with wild-type cells. In H1975 cells containing mutations in both EGFR and PIK3CA, the suppression of ATF4 induction by EGFR inhibition alone was relatively limited, but was markedly enhanced when combined with PI3K inhibition. Consequently, combined inhibition of EGFR and PI3K in double-mutant cells markedly reduced cell viability under stress conditions. These findings indicate that the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K-ATF4 axis functions as a cytoprotective mechanism under stress conditions.
To regulate ATF4 induction during amino acid deprivation, the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K pathway likely utilizes the mTOR-mediated translation control mechanisms through the eIF4F initiation complex. Of note, activation of the ISR pathway initiated by GCN2 is also essential for ATF4 induction, even in cells harboring oncogenic mutations in EGFR and PIK3CA. Unlike mTOR, GCN2 regulates translation initiation through eIF2α phosphorylation, a subunit of the eIF2 initiation complex, which is necessary to trigger the uORF-mediated ATF4 translation mechanism [6]. Thus, downstream of the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K pathway, mTOR may collaborate with GCN2 at the translation initiation level, thereby boosting ATF4 mRNA translation. A similar cooperative regulation of ATF4 induction by the GCN2-eIF2α and mTOR-eIF4F translation control mechanisms was observed in BRAF-mutated melanoma cells [18]. Although the underlying mechanisms are different, oncogenically mutated KRAS in NSCLC cells and PI3K in colorectal cancer cells enhance ATF4 expression for reprogramming amino acid metabolism [19,50]. Collectively, these findings suggest that oncogenic mutation-based mechanisms that induce ATF4 expression may be components in the management of tumor metabolic homeostasis, particularly amino acid metabolism.
Our findings may also have implications for understanding the role of concurrent mutations in EGFR and PIK3CA during metabolic regulation. Combined inhibition of EGFR and PIK3CA, compared with either alone, markedly suppressed ATF4 induction and subsequent expression of Stress-EGFR/PI3Ki signature genes under stress conditions in EGFR- and PIK3CA-mutated H1975 cells. The Stress-EGFR/PI3Ki signature contains several amino acid metabolism-related genes involved in the progression and malignancy of lung cancers, such as PSAT1 [51,52], phosphoserine phosphatase (PSPH) [53], and branched chain amino acid transaminase 1 (BCAT1) [54]. Thus, co-mutations in EGFR and PIK3CA may provide cancer cells with an advantage in adapting to amino acid-restricted conditions during tumor development. In this regard, PIK3CA mutation was shown to confer a growth advantage under osimertinib selection pressure in EGFR-mutated NSCLC cells [26]. Furthermore, the development of resistance to EGFR-TKIs often accompanies metabolic alterations, including amino acid metabolism [55]. Therefore, our discovery of ATF4-mediated metabolic adaptative mechanisms may also provide a novel explanation for the underlying mechanisms of EGFR TKI resistance occurring by co-alteration of EGFR and PIK3CA.
In conclusion, we demonstrated that the oncogenic EGFR-PI3K pathway in NSCLC cells enhances ATF4 induction to adapt to amino acid-restricted conditions, possibly through collaboration with the GCN2-initiated ISR signaling pathway. We also showed that inhibition of both oncogenically mutated EGFR and PIK3CA sensitizes NSCLC cells to amino acid deprivation. Such metabolic vulnerability may provide a novel strategy for enhancing EGFR TKI-based therapies against NSCLC. To achieve this, it will be needed to elucidate the detailed mechanisms and clinical significance of stress response regulation by the activated, mutated EGFR-PI3K pathway, using clinically relevant model systems as well as established cell lines.
